segments.title: Opening: name, address and birth
segments.summary: Amacker gives his name, spelling and address; the interviewers introduce themselves and date the recording as 1 July 1960 in New Orleans.

segments.title: Pete Lala's band: Joe Oliver, Old Man Valto, Palao
segments.summary: Amacker lists who played in the band at Pete Lala's, including Oliver, Valto, Jimmy Palao and Will Elfrey.

segments.title: Goodbyes and playing a number on the guitar
segments.summary: Farewells and chatter, then Amacker plays a piece and comments on the difficult key.

segments.title: Good blues piano players and their repertoire
segments.summary: Amacker names the old blues pianists (Sam Henry, Kitchen, Ollie Sullivan, Birmingham) and the pieces and original blues like Jelly Roll Blues they played.

segments.title: Rags and the Shithouse Rag
segments.summary: The pianists also played their own rags; Amacker describes a popular rag and who featured it, including Sam Henry and Lulu.

segments.title: Sam Henry and the public houses of the district
segments.summary: Amacker describes Sam Henry as an old Ravage Street player and the sporting houses lining the streets, with prices and some of the sex shows he took part in.

segments.title: Buddy Goins, Jockey Adams and other old pianists
segments.summary: Amacker recalls following Buddy Goins and Jockey Adams, now blind, and the interviewer asks about Robertson and Cato.

segments.title: Clarinet parts, Papa Tio, Piron and Fuclos' dance hall
segments.summary: Amacker talks about clarinet variations, Lorenzo Tio and his father, Piron and Peter Bocage, and the band he led at George Fuclos' hall on Franklin Street.

segments.title: Jimmy Noone, Arnold, and Thomas Benton
segments.summary: Talk of Jimmy Noone, a drummer called Arnold, and Thomas Benton, a guitarist and mandolin player.

segments.title: Thomas Benton's sister and Amacker's moves to Chicago and Los Angeles
segments.summary: Amacker gives dates: left New Orleans in 1919 for Chicago, to Los Angeles in January 1921, back in 1953; a bank book confirms it.

segments.title: Chicago jazz bands: Erskine Tate and Dave Payton
segments.summary: Amacker describes Chicago jazz in the early years and the bands of Erskine Tate at the Vendome and Dave Payton.

segments.title: Chicago pianists: Tony Jackson, Doc Cook, Clarence Jones
segments.summary: Amacker names the outstanding Chicago pianists and praises Tony Jackson and Charlie Cook, with Miney Jones and Clarence Jones at the Owl.

segments.title: Fate Marable, his record and Sidney Desvigne
segments.summary: Discussion of Fate Marable's one record, a claim about his calliope job, and his band with Amos White and Sidney Desvigne.

segments.title: Los Angeles piano players: Harvey Brooks
segments.summary: Amacker mentions the good pianists he found in Los Angeles, especially Harvey Brooks.

segments.title: The song 'All the Boys Love Me' and Piron
segments.summary: After naming more Los Angeles players, Amacker sings a song he composed that Piron took down, and says it was never published.

segments.title: How Piron and Johnny Sincere set the song; Amacker's sad blues
segments.summary: Amacker tells how he played the melody in the Red Light District, Piron wrote it down and Sincere added words, then sings his own blues.

segments.title: The Spikes Brothers' music store and the blues again
segments.summary: Asked about the Spikes Brothers, Amacker recalls their Central Avenue music store in Los Angeles and sings the blues again.

segments.title: Explaining the meaning of the blues
segments.summary: Amacker explains the blues as telling your woman off at home rather than fighting in public.

segments.title: Playing Joplin rags on the guitar
segments.summary: Asked about Scott Joplin, Amacker says he knew of him and played Maple Leaf Rag-type numbers on guitar.

segments.title: Harry Southard in Los Angeles and playing the blues there
segments.summary: The interviewer asks about a Los Angeles trombonist; Amacker recalls Willie Humphrey and playing his blues for women around 1921.

segments.title: Violinists: Herbert Lindsay and his double stops
segments.summary: Amacker names the greatest violinist in the city, Herbert Lindsay, called Fiddle Up, famed for his double stops.

segments.title: Buddy Bolden and the early cornet players
segments.summary: Amacker calls Buddy Bolden the loudest trumpeter, then lists Keppard, Perez, James McNeil and other early players.

segments.title: James McNeil and marches
segments.summary: McNeil was a trained player of marches like Sousa's.

segments.title: Buddy Bolden's repertoire and 'The House Got Ready'
segments.summary: Bolden played old blues; Amacker recalls tunes like Funky Butt and The House Got Ready, which got dancers wild.

segments.title: Playing professor in the sporting houses
segments.summary: Amacker explains how the house piano player worked: playing, passing the hat, and the price of drinks.

segments.title: Johnny Delpy and guitarist Frank DeLandry
segments.summary: Amacker names Johnny Delpy and praises Frank DeLandry as the greatest guitarist anywhere.
